27-far-from-the-madding-crowd:
Thomas Hardy's 1874 novel follows a shepherd, a strong-willed farmer, and the men who court her. Far from the Madding Crowd centers on Bathsheba Everdene of Weatherbury in Wessex. Gabriel Oak first loves her as a poor shepherd and later serves her farm.

Farmer Boldwood offers steady devotion, while Sergeant Troy brings charm and ruin. Fire, sheep-washing, shearing, and market days ground the love story in farm work. Bathsheba's choices carry real cost for herself and her suitors. The novel made Hardy's Wessex famous. Hardy's mix of rural detail and strong feeling set the pattern for his later Wessex novels.
445-the-crowd:
Gustave Le Bon studies the mind of crowds in this founding work of crowd psychology, arguing that people gathered for action gain new traits they lack alone. Organised crowds, he says, have always shaped history. Le Bon, a French physician, wrote The Crowd in 1895, as mass politics were rising in Europe.

Le Bon describes how suggestion, feeling, and imitation replace reason in a crowd, and how leaders guide that force. The book influenced politics and sociology for a century, and it still provokes argument about masses and power. His ideas shaped later writers on propaganda, though modern psychologists qualify his claims.
doe-osti-17135844-model-based-quantifica:
Gerry Knapp, Matthew Rolchigo, and Alex Plotkowski of Oak Ridge measure how uneven the internal structure of 3D printed 316H stainless steel can be, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4739 dated August 2026. Laser powder bed fusion builds parts layer by layer, and two parts from one machine can differ inside. For reactor use, that spread must be quantified, not guessed.

Two sources of variation are modeled. Melt pool behavior during printing shifts grain structure from spot to spot. Powder composition shifts add a second source, since small chemistry changes alter how the metal solidifies. The model based approach turns both into numbers for uniformity, giving designers a way to state expected variation. Conclusions point to future work tying the measures to part performance.
doe-osti-17135847-multi-dimensional-norm:
Andrei Savici of Oak Ridge sets out a method for normalizing powder neutron scattering data across many dimensions, in report ORNL/LTR-2026/4742 dated September 2026. In inelastic neutron experiments, detectors catch neutrons scattered by a powder sample, and raw counts must be corrected before they mean anything physical. Multi dimensional data makes that correction tricky.

Theory comes first, then implementation details. The method computes where each neutron path crosses detector and sample geometry, then assigns each crossing to the correct data bin. Each crossing contributes a known amount to the normalization total. A final chapter lists the algorithm steps in order, with notes on edge cases. The result is a recipe other reduction codes can follow exactly.
far-from-the-madding-crowd:
Thomas Hardy wrote Far from the Madding Crowd, published in 1874, the novel that first made his name. It is set in his fictional Wessex countryside. Gabriel Oak, a steady young shepherd, loses his flock in one bad night and takes work on a farm. The farm's owner is Bathsheba Everdene, proud and headstrong, whom Oak had once asked to marry him and been refused.

Bathsheba draws three very different men: Oak, the rich and brooding Farmer Boldwood, and Sergeant Troy, a dashing soldier with a hidden past and another woman's claim on him. A careless valentine, a secret marriage, and a storm over the harvest drive the tale. Hardy's love for rural work and weather fills every chapter.
the-crowd:
Gustave Le Bon subtitled The Crowd a study of the popular mind. The book opens among the titles of a criminology series from the London publisher T. Fisher Unwin, then turns to its subject: the traits of crowds. Le Bon states that his work gives an account of what crowds are like.

He argues that when people gather into a crowd for action, new mental traits appear that differ, at times sharply, from the shared traits heredity gives a race. Organized crowds have always shaped the life of peoples, he says, but never so much as now, when the blind action of crowds replaces the aware activity of single persons. He pledges a purely scientific method, free of schools, doctrines, and regard for the interests his findings may hurt.
